Education funding in pictures: the cost calendar and the monthly savings gap

Build an education reserve from annual costs, the start date, existing savings and monthly contributions. Explore four charts before choosing an account.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Hypothetical all-in education-cost budget in CAD. Costs rise annually until and during study. Savings earn the selected effective annual return, with month-end deposits, only before study. The full sum of nominal study costs is reserved when study starts, with zero return during study. No grants, tax benefits, fees, scholarships, borrowing or work income are included. This is not an RESP-benefit or institution-fee quote.

The central idea

An education goal has several payment dates. Estimate the whole cost calendar, then solve the saving requirement with explicit return and inflation assumptions.

01

Define what one study year needs to cover

Begin with an annual budget at today’s prices. Depending on the plan, that may include tuition, compulsory fees, books, supplies, housing, food, travel and equipment. A published tuition figure alone would not describe the entire cost of studying away from home.

The default CAD 20,000 is a hypothetical all-in budget, not a Canadian tuition average or an institution’s quotation. Choose an amount for a specific study plan and document what it includes. Domestic or international status, program, location, living arrangements and the number of years can all change that starting budget.

Every study year has its own price date. The cost bars inflate the starting annual budget separately to each study year. With study beginning in twelve years and 3% annual cost growth, year one costs more than today’s budget, while later study years are more expensive again. The 3% assumption is a sensitivity input, not an official education-price forecast.

02

Know what the reserve target means

This model reserves the full sum of the future nominal study costs when study begins. The reserve earns zero during study. That convention makes the cost calendar easy to inspect: each year’s nominal budget is funded at the start, without assuming investment earnings during the withdrawal period.

For annual budget C today, cost-growth rate g, y years until study and s study years, the target is Σ C(1 + g)y+k, with k running from zero to s − 1. The default four-year reserve is CAD 119,297.03. This is the total modeled funding requirement before any scholarships, grants, work income or borrowing.

A model that keeps unused funds invested during study could produce a different starting requirement and introduce additional investment risk. A monthly payment calendar could also differ from this annual illustration. Compare models only after aligning their cost dates, return assumptions and cash-flow timing.

03

Compare the selected contribution with the solved contribution

The savings chart shows two paths from the same starting balance. One uses the monthly amount selected in the controls. The other solves for the month-end contribution required to reach the reserve target by the study start date, using the same assumed effective annual return.

The default CAD 10,000 already saved plus CAD 200 per month grows to CAD 52,728.71 after twelve years at an assumed 4% annual return. The solved monthly contribution is CAD 562.59. These paths use smooth returns; they do not describe the changing value of an actual investment portfolio.

If existing savings alone already fund the target under the assumptions, the required new contribution is zero. The model does not invent a negative contribution or recommend withdrawing the excess. Future account rules, other education goals and uncertainty still need consideration.

04

Use the waterfall and matrix to locate the pressure

The waterfall adds each study year’s cost and subtracts the savings projected at the start. A positive endpoint is an unfunded reserve; a negative endpoint is a modeled surplus. Investment growth is already included in projected savings, so it must not be added again as a separate resource.

The matrix changes the years until study and the return assumption. It recalculates the future cost target for every column. A longer waiting period provides more time to save and potentially compound, but it also allows more years of cost growth. The cells show the monthly saving required after both effects.

Read several return rows rather than choosing the most convenient result. If a plan works only at a high assumed return, identify what else can change: contributions, the study budget, timing or outside funding. A higher target return brings uncertainty; it does not make the required outcome dependable.

05

Add account benefits only after checking eligibility

The Government of Canada’s education-savings overview explains RESPs and education-savings benefits. Eligibility and applicable rules require their own review. This calculator includes no grants, tax benefits, contribution limits or account withdrawal rules, and the solved contribution is not an RESP contribution recommendation.

Keep a separate dated list of confirmed outside resources. Distinguish money already available from a possible scholarship, future student employment or a loan that must be repaid. Subtracting unconfirmed resources from the goal can make the displayed gap appear smaller without improving the underlying plan.

Refresh the budget as a program and location become clearer. As the first payment approaches, review when cash must be available and how much value fluctuation the remaining horizon can tolerate. The plan should connect each cost date to an available source of money, then update as costs, family contributions and confirmed benefits change.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. The worked examples, scenario assumptions, and research checklists are TickerLantern’s own educational analysis; they are not source-reported investment results. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
